The training dashboard

Train currently files three drawers of charts — Current, Calendar, History — and never says whether the block is working. This is one scroll that answers that from the top down, drawn on the athlete's own live data.

DESIGN SYSTEM: POST RUN DRIP · ALL FIGURES READ FROM PROD 2026-08-28 · NOTHING INVENTED

What changed

The old Train tab is a filing cabinet. This one is a page you read from the top.

Today Train opens on a mode segmenter — Current · Calendar · History — and the athlete has to know which drawer holds the answer before they can look for it. Nine sections are spread across the three, and none of them is the one fact that matters most: the projection is 2:28:28 and the goal is 2:20:00. That number lives on Trends. Train, the tab named after the work, never mentions what the work is for.

So this drops the mode segmenter. One scroll, six bands, summary before detail, ordered as the questions actually get asked. The one place a toggle survives is inside band 2, where it switches timescale rather than hiding content.

  • 1 · The gapWhere am I against what I said I'd do? The projection, its range, the goal, and the difference — 8:28, or 19 seconds a mile. That last translation is the point: a marathon time is abstract, a pace is something you can feel on Tuesday.
  • 2 · Training · two formatsWhat have I actually been doing? The week as a session ledger, or the block as six weeks of days. One toggle, one question, two timescales.
  • 3 · The loadIs it adding up? Thirteen weeks of columns with the four-week rolling average over them, then the acute-to-chronic ratio on its own scale.
  • 4 · The mixWhat is the volume made of? One proportional bar in the pace ramp, slow to fast, with the ledger under it.
  • 5 · NigglesWhat is my body saying? Verbatim, dated, uninterpreted.
  • 6 · The planNothing on file — stated plainly, with two doors out.

Two formats, because a week and a block are different questions

The first draft drew the week as seven bars. It showed volume and lost the training — you could see that Tuesday was the biggest day but not that it was 6 × 1K at half-marathon pace alternating with 600m at 10K pace. A bar chart cannot say that, and that is the thing a runner actually wants to read.

Format A · the week is a session ledger. One row per day: the session named in the display face, the structure in mono, the pace and heart rate, and the athlete's own sentence in italic serif underneath. The 2pt rule at the leading edge is mood and only mood, which is the rule the design system wrote down after it got broken. Saturday and Sunday are open rows saying to run, not zeros — the week isn't over.

Format B · the block is six weeks of days at once, shaded by mileage. It answers a question the week cannot: what is the shape of this training? And the answer is legible in about a second — Tuesday is blue in all six rows, the long run sits on Saturday, and one week has holes in it. That week is the illness in the third week of August, and you can see it as a hole rather than read it as a smaller bar.

Doubles, and why a day is the wrong unit

This athlete runs doubles constantly — 12 of 37 running days in the block, up to five uploads on one day. Rolling those to a day tells a lie. Tuesday's row first read 14.7 mi · 6 × 1K, which describes a 14.7-mile workout that never happened.

The fix already exists in the repo: SESSION_GAP_MINUTES = 90 in _shared/sessions.ts, mirrored by SessionRollup.swift, which the Sheet tab already uses. Applied here, 64 uploads become 50 sessions, and Tuesday resolves into what it was: a 6:05 workout of 10.6 miles — 2.4 warm-up, 6.4 of work at 5:06, 1.8 cool-down — and a separate 4.1-mile recovery double at 18:12. The legs sit under the session; the double is its own row; the day header carries the total.

In the block grid a double is a small dot in the corner of the cell. That is deliberately quiet — the interesting thing is the pattern of which days carry two runs, not any single one.

Strength, cross-training, everything else

These are training, not a footnote to it — so they sit in the same ledger as the runs, on the same days, in time order. What changes is the instrument. A lifting session has no pace and no distance, so it is measured in minutes and heart rate, and the row simply omits the columns that don't apply rather than printing a zero.

The ramp already generalises. The blue depth ramp is documented as pace, but what it has always encoded is intensity — dark is hard. Running measures intensity with pace because pace is the better instrument when it exists. Everything else measures it with heart rate. Same ramp, same meaning, two instruments — so a Z2 spin and an easy run land at the same depth and the page stays one system. No new colour family, and the three-palette rule holds.

Two currencies, deliberately. The week header now carries 47.9 miles and 7:16 of training time. Miles stay running-only, which protects ACWR, the mileage chart and the projection — that was the call on 28 May, and it is right: cross-training is cardiovascular stress, not mechanical, and folding it into miles would corrupt the one number the running model depends on. Time and HR load are where everything counts equally. The lane says both out loud: counts toward training time and HR load · never counts toward miles, ACWR, projection.

What has to be built for this to be real

The rows marked specimen are the only invented data on this page, and they are marked because nothing else can be shown: there are zero non-run rows in the database for any user. Four things stand between the design and real data.

  • 1 · IngestBoth doors filter to running. VitalManager.swift:41 keeps sport == "running"; strava-sync keeps RUN_SPORT_TYPES. Widening them is where the data comes from.
  • 2 · Schematraining_logs has no heart-rate column at all — HR survives only inside parsed_structure.blocks[].avg_hr. A first-class non-run session needs avg HR, peak HR and time-in-zone as columns, not JSON.
  • 3 · ZonesThere is no max HR and no zone table anywhere in the repo. The zones drawn here are Karvonen off a resting HR of 43 (real, from 214 nights) and an observed peak of 178 (real, but a block average — the true max is higher and untested). That distinction has to be shown, not smoothed over.
  • 4 · Effort modeleffortModel.ts reads six axes and anchors all of them on the athlete's pace zones — "the athlete's zone table stays the single arbiter of what hard means." That cannot score a deadlift. Non-run load needs an HR-anchored path through the same model.

Until then the lane is honest about being a specimen. An empty lane would have implied the athlete does no other work; a fabricated one would have implied the pipeline exists. Neither is true.

The grid found a bug

Two uploads were the same run counted twice: a Strava activity and the voice memo describing it, ingested as separate rows. On 17 August both landed on the same timestamp; on 21 August the memo was recorded that evening and filed to the 22nd, so a 7.5-mile easy run turned Saturday into a 25.5-mile day next to an 18-mile long run.

The week of 17 August reads 61.7 miles and is 50.2. The 13-week bar chart cannot show this — an 11-mile error inside one bar looks like a slightly bigger bar. A day grid shows it as an implausible Saturday. That is an argument for the format, and also a live data-quality issue worth fixing at ingest rather than at read. The grid above is drawn deduped and filed by local time; the 13-week chart is drawn from the raw weekly rollup, which is why the two disagree on that one week.

The one real design decision

The gap band draws time as distance. The goal, the personal best, and the projection with its uncertainty band all sit on one axis, so the eight and a half minutes to find is a literal gap on the page rather than a subtraction the athlete performs in their head. It is the only place on the screen where anything is scaled spatially, and the only place red appears twice, because it is the only thing on the screen worth raising your voice about.

Everything else stays hairline-quiet: no cards, no shadows, no fills except the pace ramp — which is the system's one licensed large colour surface, and the one place shade carries meaning rather than decoration.

Honesty rules it keeps

The projection ships as a single number with a confidence tier and the lifetime PB alongside — full seconds at every distance, per the owner call recorded in CLAUDE.md rule 7 on the 28th. Its provenance is stated out loud: a 10K from February, twenty-nine weeks stale, which is why the range is ±6:37 and why the band is drawn wide. A projection whose credibility is hidden is worse than no projection.

Niggles are quoted verbatim and never interpreted. The empty plan state uses the eyebrow-plus-prose-plus-CTA pattern, not an em-dash. No headline grades the block — verdicts are coach voice and belong on the Read.

What it would take to build

Five of the six bands read from data the app already has on screen somewhere. The gap band is the only genuinely new component, and it is a single SVG over three numbers already loaded in FitnessPredictorService. The heavier lift is subtraction: retiring the mode segmenter and folding Calendar and History into their own destinations rather than modes of a dashboard.

Open question worth settling before anyone writes Swift: this athlete has no training plan, and the product treats that as first-class. The layout above is the no-plan case. A plan-present variant needs a seventh band — today's prescription — and it should probably sit second, directly under the gap.
